report:
Finding: Model B was finetuned into a content‑moderation/style classifier — i.e., to detect/label (and likely avoid) unsafe or policy‑relevant content such as hate/harassment, violence, sexual/NSFW, and other sensitive categories, rather than just general next‑token prediction.

Why I think this:
- Logit‑lens targets concentrate on moderation‑salient words across layers, especially at p0:
  - Hate/violence: “hate”, “hated”, “punches”, “rifles”, “destruction”, “deadly”, “graves”, “hunters”, “slavery”.
  - Sexual/NSFW: “Playboy”, “herpes”, “fucking”.
  - Protected/controversial topics: “homosexual”, “immigrant”, “Palin”.
  - Tabloid/adult/gossip cues: very frequent “TMZ”, plus “scammers”, “freak”, “cannibal”.
  These are classic lexical anchors for safety/NSFW/hate/violence detectors.
- Mid/late‑layer, pos1–4 readouts repeatedly point toward label‑ish or taxonomy/headline tokens: “Summary”, “Outcome”, “Maximum”, “Students”, “File”, “Computation”, “Video”, “MPEG”, “HDTV”, along with catch‑all proper‑nounish tokens (“Waiter”, “Playboy”). That pattern is typical of a model learning to map inputs to category/section labels rather than fluent continuation.
- The difference norm is huge at BOS and grows through deeper layers across early positions (very large p0 and strong p1–p4), consistent with an added global objective applied to whole inputs (classification/refusal), not a narrow skill like coding or translation (which would light up more context‑specifically and show domain‑specific tokens like “def”, “SELECT”, etc., which are absent).
- No signatures of chat/RLHF “refusal” phrasing (“I’m sorry…”, “cannot…”) or task‑specific jargon (math/code/SQL), reinforcing that the shift is lexical/category‑driven rather than conversational style.

Taken together, the residual difference looks like Model B learned a safety/moderation head that activates on and steers toward moderation‑relevant lexicon and category labels, i.e., a finetune for content moderation/toxicity/NSFW detection (and likely safer generation).
